screens.title: Ensuring Compliance and Governance with AWS Config
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will treat AWS Config as the continuous observer and auditor of your cloud environment. You will learn how Config records the exact configuration of supported resources over time, why that historical view matters for root cause analysis and audits, and how rules provide automated compliance checks. We will work with both AWS managed rules and custom rules driven by Lambda functions, and we will cover practical integrations with SNS, Lambda, Security Hub, and Control Tower. You’ll also get a hands-on activity that shows a managed rule detecting a deliberately public S3 bucket and the timeline you use for investigation. By the end of this chapter you should be able to configure the recorder, reason about configuration items and timelines, choose between managed and custom rules, and design safe remediation patterns. Keep in mind a common pitfall: recording too broadly or automating remediation without testing can cause cost surprises or operational disruption. As we proceed, think about what resources in your accounts you must always record and which rules would prevent your common misconfigurations.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Overview
Ensuring Compliance and Governance with AWS Config
Continuous monitoring, evaluation, and remediation to keep cloud resources compliant and auditable.
In this lesson
Understand Config's recorder, configuration items, managed and custom rules, integrations, and safe remediation patterns through a guided lab.
Why it matters
Config gives you the continuous audit trail needed for security investigations and governance, letting you answer who changed what and when.

Recording & CIs
How Config records configuration items and builds a timeline for each resource.
Rules & Evaluation
Managed and custom rules evaluate resources and mark non-compliant items.
Integrations

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to configure AWS Config to continuously record resource configurations, evaluate those resources using both managed and custom rules, and integrate compliance events with other services. First, you will learn to enable the configuration recorder and select the correct resource types and regions to avoid blind spots or excessive costs. Second, you’ll understand the structure of a configuration item and how the timeline supports forensic analysis. Third, you will be able to deploy managed Config Rules, like the pre-built rule that flags public S3 buckets, and interpret compliance results. Finally, you will design simple custom rules using Lambda to enforce specific tagging or runtime policies. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic to help you remember: record, timeline, rules, and extend. These skills are practical for audits, incident response, and maintaining governance across accounts. As you progress, reflect on which resources in your environment must always be recorded and which checks will prevent your most common misconfigurations.

screens.title: What is AWS Config?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config is a managed service that records the configuration state of supported AWS resources as configuration items, creating a continuous, point-in-time history. Think of it as both a camera and a ledger: it captures how resources are configured and preserves that state so you can inspect it later. This history is crucial when you need to answer who changed a setting, when it happened, and what the configuration looked like before and after the change. For example, if an S3 bucket becomes publicly readable, Config’s configuration items let you see when the public access setting changed and which configuration persisted before that change. A common misconception is that Config replaces CloudTrail; it does not. CloudTrail logs A P I calls and the actor, while Config records the resulting resource configuration. You often need both: CloudTrail tells you who performed the change, and Config shows the exact resource state over time. Key takeaway: Config provides the continuous, queryable record of resource state required for audit, compliance reporting, and forensic troubleshooting. What is AWS Config? means aws config records resource configurations as configuration items, building a historical timeline for auditing and troubleshooting.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and why continuous configuration history matters.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › What is AWS Config?
Definition & Purpose
AWS Config captures and stores point-in-time configuration items for supported AWS resources, creating a timeline useful for governance and troubleshooting.
Analogy
Like a security camera plus an auditor: records state and keeps the record for later inspection.
Misconception
Config is not a replacement for CloudTrail; use Config for state and CloudTrail for API actors.
Why it matters
Audits and forensic investigations depend on accurate, historical configuration data to trace incidents and verify compliance.
Key Takeaway

Config is the canonical historical view of resource configuration; pair it with CloudTrail for complete audit context.

Configuration Item (CI) Example
{
  "resourceType": "AWS::S3::Bucket",
  "resourceId": "my-public-config-test-bucket",
  "configuration": {
    "publicAccessBlock": false,
    "bucketPolicy": "..."
  },
  "captureTime": "2026-01-01T12:34:56Z"
}
Each CI contains the resource’s attributes at a point in time. Use the timeline to compare successive CIs when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Configuration Recorder and Recording Scope
screens.narratorSegment: The configuration recorder is the component that tells AWS Config which supported resource types and which regions to observe. When enabled, the recorder captures each resource’s configuration and sends it to the configured S3 bucket and optionally to CloudWatch Events for near-real-time processing. Choosing the right recording scope is an operational decision: recording all resource types in all regions gives maximum visibility but increases storage and evaluation costs. A common practical approach is to record all resources in production accounts and limit non-production accounts to a narrower set of critical resource types. For example, record S3, EC2, RDS, IAM, and Lambda in production, but only S3 and IAM in development if you need lower cost. Misconfiguration to avoid: do not enable recording in every region by default if your organization never uses those regions; this can create noise and extra cost. Key operational steps are: create the service-linked role, enable the recorder, select S3 bucket and delivery options, and confirm the resource types. Always validate the recorder by creating a test change and checking the resource timeline. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Recorder & Scope
1. Create service-linked role
Config needs a role to record and deliver CIs to S3 and other services.
2. Enable recorder
Select regions and resource types you want to record.
3. Choose delivery
Pick an S3 bucket to store CIs and enable SNS/CloudWatch Events if needed.
Why it matters

The recorder defines what you can audit. Bad scope choices mean blind spots or unexpected costs.

Scope Trade-offs
Wide scope (all resources)
Pros: Complete visibility for audits. Cons: Higher storage, more evaluations, and potential cost.
Targeted scope
Pros: Lower cost and less noise. Cons: Possible blind spots if you miss a resource type.
Quick validation
Make a small configuration change, then open the resource's timeline in Config to confirm a new configuration item was recorded and contains expected attributes.

screens.title: Managed Rules vs Custom Rules
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config Rules come in two forms: managed rules provided by AWS for common compliance checks, and custom rules implemented with Lambda when you need organization-specific logic. Managed rules are quick to deploy and cover frequent needs such as ensuring S3 buckets are not publicly readable or that EBS volumes are encrypted. They are maintained by AWS and are a good first line of defense. Custom rules are appropriate when your organization requires checks AWS doesn’t provide, for example ensuring instances launched in a particular VPC have a specific tag or enforcing runtime versions for Lambda functions. Custom rules give you full control over evaluation logic but require a Lambda function, careful testing, and attention to potential performance or false positive issues. A common misconception is that custom rules are always better because they are tailored; in fact, managed rules reduce maintenance overhead and are less likely to introduce runtime complications. The practical pattern is to use managed rules where they apply and reserve custom rules for gaps in coverage. Managed Rules vs Custom Rules means use managed rules for standard checks; use custom lambda-backed rules when you require bespoke, organization-specific evaluations.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Managed vs Custom Rules
Managed Rules
Pre-built by AWS to check common best practices. Quick to deploy and low maintenance.
  • Examples: S3 public access checks, EBS encryption.
  • Pros: maintained by AWS, lower operational burden.
  • Cons: may not cover organization-specific needs.
Tip

Search for a managed rule before building a custom one to save effort.

Custom Rules (Lambda)
Use Lambda to implement logic that evaluates resources against bespoke policies, such as tag presence or runtime constraints.
  • Pros: full control and tailored checks.
  • Cons: requires Lambda code, testing, and careful IAM permissions.
  • Watch out for false positives and Lambda time limits when evaluating many resources.
Common mistake

Creating too many untested custom rules can produce noise and unexpected Lambda costs.

screens.title: Example: Managed Rule JSON and S3 Non-Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: Here we examine a representative managed rule definition and the practical S3 bucket scenario used in the hands-on activity. The managed rule is a metadata object that tells Config which resource types to evaluate and which built-in evaluator to run. For S3 public access, the rule flags a bucket if its ACL or policy allows public read. In practice you add this rule in the Config console; Config will then evaluate every S3 bucket in scope and mark non-compliant resources. The lab walks you through creating a bucket without the block-public-access guardrails and applying a bucket policy that allows public reads. After a few minutes, the managed rule evaluates and marks that bucket non-compliant. Use the Config console to inspect the rule’s resources-in-scope and click the resource’s timeline to view the configuration items that show the change. Important operational note: allow time for evaluation to complete and use the timeline to correlate with CloudTrail events to identify who made the change. keyIdea.text: Managed rule metadata defines scope and source; use timelines and resources-in-scope to find and investigate non-compliant buckets.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Managed Rule Example
Managed Rule Object
{
  "ConfigRuleName": "s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited",
  "Description": "Checks if S3 buckets are publicly readable.",
  "Scope": {
    "ComplianceResourceTypes": ["AWS::S3::Bucket"]
  },
  "Source": {
    "Owner": "AWS",
    "SourceIdentifier": "S3_BUCKET_PUBLIC_READ_PROHIBITED"
  }
}
This JSON configures Config to run the built-in S3 public-read evaluator over S3 buckets in scope.
S3 Non-Compliance Scenario
Create a bucket with public read enabled and the managed rule will mark it non-compliant after evaluation.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name/*"
    }
  ]
}
After the change, examine the resource’s timeline to see when the configuration changed and pair with CloudTrail to find the actor.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Deploying the Managed Rule and Triggering Non-Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab shows the exact steps to enable AWS Config, add the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited managed rule, and create a deliberately non-compliant S3 bucket to observe the result. Start by enabling AWS Config in the console and create or select a delivery S3 bucket and a service-linked role. Choose to record all resources for the demo or restrict to S3 if you want to reduce noise. Next, open Rules in Config and add the managed rule named s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited. The rule will begin evaluating. Then, in S3 create a bucket with block public access turned off and add a bucket policy allowing public get object. Wait a few minutes and refresh the Config Rules page; the rule should show a non-compliant resource. Click the rule and then the non-compliant resource to view the timeline. The timeline contains configuration items showing the change that made the bucket public. Finally, correlate the timestamp with CloudTrail to see who made the change. After completing the experiment, remember to delete the public bucket and remove the rule to avoid security risks and unexpected charges. screens.title: Integrating Config with SNS, Lambda, and Security Hub
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config does not operate in isolation; its value is amplified when you route compliance events to other services. A common pattern is Config Rule -> SNS -> Lambda. When a rule flags non-compliance, Config can publish the change to SNS. An SNS subscription triggers a Lambda function that can perform read-only actions for investigation or attempt a remediation action such as changing a bucket ACL back to private. Before enabling automated remediation, perform extensive testing in non-production and ensure the Lambda role has least-privilege permissions. Additionally, integrating Config with Security Hub centralizes findings across multiple security services, making it easier for security teams to triage alerts. AWS Control Tower can consume Config outputs for multi-account governance and help enforce organizational guardrails. A typical architecture boxes Config as the detector, SNS as the dispatcher, Lambda as the remediator, and Security Hub as the aggregator. Always include an approval or throttling mechanism in automated remediation to avoid rapid unintended changes in production environments. Integrating Config with SNS, Lambda, and Security Hub means use config events with sns and lambda for notifications and remediation, and forward findings to security hub for centralized governance.. In practical terms, notification, automated remediation, and centralized security posture.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Configuration Items and the Compliance Timeline
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration Items, or CIs, are the atomic records AWS Config stores for each supported resource each time it changes or when periodic snapshots occur. Each CI contains the resource identifier, a capture time, and the full configuration attributes relevant to that resource type. Over time those CIs form a timeline you can play back to understand how a resource evolved. This timeline is essential for forensic analysis: combine it with CloudTrail to discover who initiated a change and Config to see exactly what changed. A practical example is investigating why a database lost encryption. The timeline will show the CI where encryption was disabled and the preceding CI where it was enabled, letting you compare field values. A common misunderstanding is expecting CIs to include unrelated metadata like cost allocation tags unless those tags are part of the resource configuration; confirm which attributes are captured for each resource type. screens.title: Safe Remediation and IAM Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Automated remediation is powerful but must be handled with care. The recommended pattern is to pilot remediation in a staging account, log all actions, and implement a throttling or approval mechanism before enabling automatic changes in production. When a Config rule triggers a Lambda remediation, the Lambda function requires permissions to change the resource. Apply the principle of least privilege: grant the Lambda only the actions it needs on the specific resource types and avoid wildcards in resource ARNs. Another critical area is error handling: your Lambda remediation should handle transient failures gracefully and write detailed logs for post-incident review. A common mistake is giving remediation code overly broad permissions and then enabling it globally; this can cause cascading outages. Also, monitor costs associated with frequent evaluations and Lambda invocations and consider rate limits. Final tip: instrument remediation with explicit dry-run modes and human approval steps for high-risk changes. screens.title: Using Config for Security Investigations
screens.narratorSegment: When a security team detects an unexpected exposure, AWS Config helps you answer three critical questions: what changed, when did it change, and what was the previous state. Start by locating the non-compliant resource in Config and open its timeline. The timeline shows CIs with timestamps you can compare to identify the exact change in configuration. Then consult CloudTrail events near that timestamp to discover the IAM principal who performed the action. This combination provides both the configuration context and the actor. For example, if an S3 bucket unexpectedly becomes public, Config shows the CI where public access is enabled and the prior CI where it was not; CloudTrail shows which IAM role or user executed the A P I call that caused the change. Remember to check whether automated processes or remediation jobs could have made the change. A frequent mistake is assuming human action by default; always verify whether an automation pipeline or Lambda may have altered the resource. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will treat AWS Config as the continuous observer and auditor of your cloud environment. You will learn how Config records the exact configuration of supported resources over time, why that historical view matters for root cause analysis and audits, and how rules provide automated compliance checks. We will work with both AWS managed rules and custom rules driven by Lambda functions, and we will cover practical integrations with SNS, Lambda, Security Hub, and Control Tower. You’ll also get a hands-on activity that shows a managed rule detecting a deliberately public S3 bucket and the timeline you use for investigation. By the end of this chapter you should be able to configure the recorder, reason about configuration items and timelines, choose between managed and custom rules, and design safe remediation patterns. Keep in mind a common pitfall: recording too broadly or automating remediation without testing can cause cost surprises or operational disruption. As we proceed, think about what resources in your accounts you must always record and which rules would prevent your common misconfigurations.

By the end of these screens you will be able to configure AWS Config to continuously record resource configurations, evaluate those resources using both managed and custom rules, and integrate compliance events with other services. First, you will learn to enable the configuration recorder and select the correct resource types and regions to avoid blind spots or excessive costs. Second, you’ll understand the structure of a configuration item and how the timeline supports forensic analysis. Third, you will be able to deploy managed Config Rules, like the pre-built rule that flags public S3 buckets, and interpret compliance results. Finally, you will design simple custom rules using Lambda to enforce specific tagging or runtime policies. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic to help you remember: record, timeline, rules, and extend. These skills are practical for audits, incident response, and maintaining governance across accounts. As you progress, reflect on which resources in your environment must always be recorded and which checks will prevent your most common misconfigurations.

This second objectives screen focuses on extending AWS Config into operational workflows and avoiding common pitfalls. You will learn to connect Config change and compliance events to Amazon SNS for notifications and to Lambda for safe, automated remediation. You will also understand how Config feeds findings into broader services like Security Hub and AWS Control Tower for multi-account governance. Another objective is to identify the right scope of recording to balance visibility and costs: choosing resource types and regions deliberately avoids missing critical resources or creating excessive events. Finally, you will practice safety patterns: test remediation logic in non-production, apply least-privilege roles for Config and Lambda, and avoid over-automating changes that could cause outages. These objectives give you actionable patterns for governance and a checklist to avoid common operational risks.

AWS Config is a managed service that records the configuration state of supported AWS resources as configuration items, creating a continuous, point-in-time history. Think of it as both a camera and a ledger: it captures how resources are configured and preserves that state so you can inspect it later. This history is crucial when you need to answer who changed a setting, when it happened, and what the configuration looked like before and after the change. For example, if an S3 bucket becomes publicly readable, Config’s configuration items let you see when the public access setting changed and which configuration persisted before that change. A common misconception is that Config replaces CloudTrail; it does not. CloudTrail logs A P I calls and the actor, while Config records the resulting resource configuration. You often need both: CloudTrail tells you who performed the change, and Config shows the exact resource state over time. Key takeaway: Config provides the continuous, queryable record of resource state required for audit, compliance reporting, and forensic troubleshooting. What is AWS Config? means aws config records resource configurations as configuration items, building a historical timeline for auditing and troubleshooting.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and why continuous configuration history matters.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The configuration recorder is the component that tells AWS Config which supported resource types and which regions to observe. When enabled, the recorder captures each resource’s configuration and sends it to the configured S3 bucket and optionally to CloudWatch Events for near-real-time processing. Choosing the right recording scope is an operational decision: recording all resource types in all regions gives maximum visibility but increases storage and evaluation costs. A common practical approach is to record all resources in production accounts and limit non-production accounts to a narrower set of critical resource types. For example, record S3, EC2, RDS, IAM, and Lambda in production, but only S3 and IAM in development if you need lower cost. Misconfiguration to avoid: do not enable recording in every region by default if your organization never uses those regions; this can create noise and extra cost. Key operational steps are: create the service-linked role, enable the recorder, select S3 bucket and delivery options, and confirm the resource types. Always validate the recorder by creating a test change and checking the resource timeline. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS Config Rules come in two forms: managed rules provided by AWS for common compliance checks, and custom rules implemented with Lambda when you need organization-specific logic. Managed rules are quick to deploy and cover frequent needs such as ensuring S3 buckets are not publicly readable or that EBS volumes are encrypted. They are maintained by AWS and are a good first line of defense. Custom rules are appropriate when your organization requires checks AWS doesn’t provide, for example ensuring instances launched in a particular VPC have a specific tag or enforcing runtime versions for Lambda functions. Custom rules give you full control over evaluation logic but require a Lambda function, careful testing, and attention to potential performance or false positive issues. A common misconception is that custom rules are always better because they are tailored; in fact, managed rules reduce maintenance overhead and are less likely to introduce runtime complications. The practical pattern is to use managed rules where they apply and reserve custom rules for gaps in coverage. Automated remediation is powerful but must be handled with care. The recommended pattern is to pilot remediation in a staging account, log all actions, and implement a throttling or approval mechanism before enabling automatic changes in production. When a Config rule triggers a Lambda remediation, the Lambda function requires permissions to change the resource. Apply the principle of least privilege: grant the Lambda only the actions it needs on the specific resource types and avoid wildcards in resource ARNs. Another critical area is error handling: your Lambda remediation should handle transient failures gracefully and write detailed logs for post-incident review. A common mistake is giving remediation code overly broad permissions and then enabling it globally; this can cause cascading outages. Also, monitor costs associated with frequent evaluations and Lambda invocations and consider rate limits. Final tip: instrument remediation with explicit dry-run modes and human approval steps for high-risk changes. When a security team detects an unexpected exposure, AWS Config helps you answer three critical questions: what changed, when did it change, and what was the previous state. Start by locating the non-compliant resource in Config and open its timeline. The timeline shows CIs with timestamps you can compare to identify the exact change in configuration. Then consult CloudTrail events near that timestamp to discover the IAM principal who performed the action. This combination provides both the configuration context and the actor. For example, if an S3 bucket unexpectedly becomes public, Config shows the CI where public access is enabled and the prior CI where it was not; CloudTrail shows which IAM role or user executed the A P I call that caused the change. These key concepts capture the essentials you should remember from this chapter. AWS Config is the service that records resource configurations and produces configuration items. A configuration item is a timestamped snapshot of a resource’s attributes. Config Rules evaluate resources against desired baselines and can be either AWS managed or custom Lambda-backed rules. Keep these definitions in mind as you design governance and incident response processes because they are the vocabulary you will use to reason about compliance, audits, and remediation. Make sure you can explain each term in one sentence and give a short example: for instance, a Config Rule that flags public S3 buckets or a CI that shows an EC2 instance’s security groups at a given time. These concise definitions make communication with auditors and security teams precise and actionable.

These final concept cards capture operational checks and governance hygiene. Managed Rules are the first option for common compliance needs because they are maintained by AWS and require minimal maintenance. Custom Rules use Lambda to evaluate bespoke policies that managed rules do not cover, but they demand testing and careful IAM controls. Remediation Actions are automated responses to non-compliance; always test them in staging and use least-privilege roles. The Configuration Recorder is the switch that determines what Config observes and must be scoped thoughtfully to manage cost and visibility. Keep these operational points in mind when designing your compliance program to ensure it is effective, safe, and maintainable.
